512	                                   gravity or thirst, we analyzed the data in Tables 1 and 2. Both the relationship between body mass change and urine
513	                                   specific gravity (r = 0.50, p = 0.013), as well as the relationship between body mass change and rating of thirst (r = 0.68,
514	                                   p = 0.001), were significantly correlated. The strength of these two relationships are interpreted as fair and moderately
515	                                   strong, respectively.107,117
516	                                       The findings described in the three previous paragraphs demonstrate that our three criterion hydration biomarkers
517	                                   responded consistently when a body water deficit occurred; this suggests satisfactory internal validity. Two individual
518	                                   exceptions to this observation appear in Table 3, in the form of cyclists who experienced exertional hyponatremia during
519	                                   a 164-km summer ultraendurance event. Row 1 of Table 3 shows that the comparison group with normal serum sodium
520	                                   levels (column 4) consumed an average of 5.9 L of fluid during 9.0 h of cycling. In contrast, the hyponatremic cyclists
521	                                   A and B consumed 13.7 L/8.9 h and 14.7 L/10.6 h, respectively, which resulted in serum sodium concentrations of
522	                                   130 mmol/L for both27 – well below the range observed among healthy adults (136–145 mmol/L).67 In terms of body
523	                                   mass, the comparison group lost 1.3%, cyclist A gained 4.3%, and cyclist B experienced virtually no change of body
524	                                   mass (+0.1%). This obvious difference among the two hyponatremic cyclists (ie, who had identical pre- and post-ride
525	                                   serum sodium values) likely resulted from a large difference in their sweat rates and the fact that cyclist B rode
526	                                   1.7 h longer than cyclist A. It is noteworthy that both cyclists A and B exhibited post-ride urine specific gravities and
527	                                   thirst ratings that were well below the mean values of the comparison group (column 4). This illustrates an important
528	                                   concept. Due to the complex interactions of many factors, some cases of exertional hyponatremia involve body mass gain
529	                                   (ie, overhydration and water retention that exceeds sweat, urine, and respiratory water losses),118,119 whereas other cases
530	                                   are associated with a large unreplaced sweat sodium loss and partially-replaced water loss.120–122 Thus, the development
531	                                   of exertional hyponatremia in cyclists A and B (Table 3) and the responses of hydration biomarkers were idiosyncratic.27
532	
533	                                   Considerations for Developing an IHP
534	                                   Previous publications describe (a) the negative effects which fluid–electrolyte imbalances can have on athletic perfor­
535	                                   mance, physiological functions, and health;3,4,46,51 and (b) the importance of developing an IHP for each athlete,123 as
536	                                   opposed to utilizing a single hydration biomarker value or a narrow range of values to indicate the threshold of
537	                                   detrimental effects for all athletes.84,98 In its simplest form, an IHP involves measuring an athlete’s sweat rate (described
538	                                   in the section titled “Body mass”) and planning the appropriate volume and timing of fluid intake in view of the
539	                                   anticipated rehydration opportunities of the sport. More sophisticated IHP models take into account an athlete’s tolerance
540	                                   to consuming a relatively large fluid volume,41 the concentration of electrolytes in sweat (ie, sodium, chloride,
541	                                   potassium),124,125 or the events that require sodium and carbohydrate in rehydration fluids.51,122,126 An IHP that
542	                                   incorporates most or all of these factors increases the likelihood that an athlete will attain the desirable middle ground
543	                                   between underhydration and overhydration, thereby optimizing performance.
544	
545	                                   Interpreting Biomarker Data
546	                                   The hydration biomarker data in Tables 1–5 are intended to be used concurrently with other information to interpret changes
547	                                   of hydration status. Because no single biomarker accurately indicates hydration status for all athletes, activities, and
548	                                   environments, and because different biomarkers sometimes provide conflicting information (ie, due to the dynamic
549	                                   complexity of human fluid–electrolyte regulation29–33), it is best to employ information from multiple sources to determine
550	                                   hydration status.31–55 One common technique involves comparing an athlete’s biomarker information to a single static
551	                                   value that represents the threshold of detrimental effects attributed to dehydration; in fact, most sport nutrition and human
552	                                   hydration publications4,44–50 provide a single biomarker value (eg, urine specific gravity of 1.020) or a narrow range of
553	                                   values (eg, body mass loss of 3–4%) for all athletes, activities, and environments. As a second source of information, each
554	                                   athlete can maintain a personal diary of body weight, urine specific gravity, and thirst measurements, before and after
555	                                   exercise; with this data, he/she can monitor trends across days and weeks to develop personalized reference values
556	                                   representing usual body weight changes, urine specific gravities, and thirst ratings. This diary of past hydration experiences
557	                                   can then be compared to each new competition or daily training session. The biomarker data of the present review
558	                                   represents a third source of information. Tables 1–5 provide activity-specific values which can be utilized by athletes,

                                     e
                                   2; Participants marked a visual analog scale (100 mm straight line flanked by “not at all” on the left side and “very” on the right) in response to the question “How thirsty are you?”



                                       Figure 2 provides a visual summary of the hydration biomarker data (group averages) contained in Tables 1 and 5. As
                                   such, it illustrates net body water loss during athletic competition or training, as well as water restriction during daily
                                   activities that include no exercise. All thirst ratings and urine specific gravity values in Figure 2 increased when a net
                                   body water loss occurred (ie, body mass decreased). Figure 3 further illustrates the association among the criterion
                                   biomarker data (group averages) from the research studies presented in Tables 1–5.


                                   Discussion
                                   The evidence gathered by the present narrative review illustrates a wide range of hydration biomarker changes (ie, shown
                                   as standard deviations from the mean) which men and women experience during competition, training, and routine daily
                                   activities. Although not within the scope of the present study, from the assessed literature it is evident that this sizeable
                                   variability results from interactions of (a) sport-specific exercise mode, duration, and intensity; (b) individual differences
                                   of heat acclimatization status, fluid-electrolyte losses in sweat, physical training history, personal knowledge or beliefs

                                   Figure 2 A visual summary of body mass, thirst rating, and urine specific gravity changes due to net body water loss during various activities. The 10 color-coded symbols
                                   represent the athletic competitions and training sessions described in Table 1. White symbols denote the 24-h period of water restriction during routine daily activities (n = 14)
                                   with no exercise, as described in Table 5 (columns 2 to 4). All symbols represent group averages (range, n = 6–57). Abbreviation: VAS, visual analog scale.




                                   Figure 3 Relationships among the three hydration-relevant variables of this review: thirst, body mass loss, and urine specific gravity. Data points are mean values from the
                                   studies cited in Tables 1–5. Test participants rated thirst using either a 100-mm visual analog scale (left vertical axis) or a 9-point category scale (right vertical axis) in panels
                                   (A) and (B). Percent female sex: panel (A), 21%, panel (B), 8%, panel (C), 8%.



                                   about rehydration during exercise; (c) intentional water loss by athletes who attempt to “make weight”; (d) gear or
                                   clothing insulation; and (e) environmental conditions.31,51–54,71,72 This complexity and variability make it difficult to
                                   accurately predict in advance the fluid deficit or excess which any athlete might encounter during training or
                                   competition.19,42,73,74 Thus, investigators and professional organizations recommend creating an individualized plan
                                   for each athlete.3,4,19,30,34,56,73,75–77 However, previous investigations have not succeeded in providing practical, indivi­
                                   dualized hydration guidelines for athletes,76 few inventories of hydration biomarker reference values have been
                                   published, and none of those studies examined the hydration biomarker responses of athletes during training, competi­
                                   tion, overhydration, or purposeful weight loss for multiple sports76,78–80 as are presented in Tables 1–3. Also, in most
                                   publications, a single hydration biomarker measurement (eg, urine specific gravity of 1.020) or a narrow range of values

                                   (eg, body mass loss of 3–4%) represents the threshold of detrimental effects for all athletes.1,4,46,81–83 This approach does
                                   not take into account the large variability of hydration biomarker values shown in Tables 1–5.
                                       Optimal IHPs incorporate biomarkers that are easy-to-use, field expedient, noninvasive, safe, portable, and
                                   inexpensive.3,4,30,34,75,77 In view of these criteria, several hydration biomarkers were initially considered for inclusion
                                   in the present review,34,37,39,84 including clinical assessment methods.35 The following five points influenced our decision
                                   to employ three hydration biomarkers: body mass change, urine specific gravity, and subjective rating of thirst. First, the
                                   2022 consensus statement of the International Olympic Committee Medical and Scientific Commission recommended
                                   that athletes monitor their body weight, urine specific gravity (or urine color), and thirst during periods of training or
                                   competing in hot environments.82 Second, an evaluation of 13 hydration assessment methods determined that body mass
                                   change, urine specific gravity, and rating of thirst were among the top five most suitable field techniques;34 the criteria for
                                   this finding were cost and time of analysis, technical expertise required, portability, and likelihood of an adverse event.
                                   Third, acute body mass change is recognized as the simplest and most accurate index of hydration status when serial
                                   measurements are collected in close proximity (eg, pre- and post-exercise, ≤ 4h) and when corrected for the mass of urine
                                   excreted and fluid consumed during the activity.4,34,85–88 Fourth, human body water balance primarily depends on two
                                   parameters: thirst that influences input, and urine excretion that determines output. When a deficit or excess of total body
                                   water exists, the kidneys act to restore euhydration. As a result, a change of urine concentration (eg, specific gravity) can
                                   distinguish a net loss or gain of body water (Figure 2), discriminate between euhydration and dehydration,4,27,89,90 and
                                   determine whether daily total water intake is adequate.68,91–93 Fifth, measurements of body mass, urine specific gravity,
                                   and thirst each have limitations when they are employed alone to assess hydration state, due to factors such as time
                                   of day, internal circadian rhythms, first morning hydration state, and dietary osmolar load.3,94–96 For example, consump­
                                   tion of a large bolus of water or a high protein diet may alter urine specific gravity acutely.30,97,98 Also, the intensity of
                                   thirst may be difficult to replicate consistently on a rating scale due to the interactions of numerous internal physiologic
                                   (eg, plasma osmolality and volume, oropharyngeal sensations) and external (eg, fluid characteristics, learned preferences,
                                   air temperature) influencing factors which are integrated by the brain.32,33,59,94–106 Therefore, we conclude that a single
                                   hydration assessment method (a) is not valid in all scenarios or for all individuals,34–39 and (b) does not provide
                                   unequivocal evidence of fluid intake inadequacy.31 However, research studies have shown that the combination of two
                                   hydration biomarkers makes identification of inadequate fluid intake or dehydration likely, and the combination of three
                                   indices makes this determination very likely.31,55,70

                                   Hydration Biomarker Interrelationships
                                   Figure 2 provides a visual summary of body mass changes (%), subjective thirst ratings, and urine specific gravity values
                                   from 12 studies which focused on outdoor athletic competitions or training sessions (Table 1), and 24-h water restriction
                                   during routine daily activities (Table 5). All symbols represent group means (n = 6–28) and illustrate consistent
                                   agreement among these three hydration indices, in that all thirst ratings increased and all urine specific gravity values
                                   increased when a net body water loss occurred (ie, body mass decreased).
                                       Figure 3 illustrates the relationships of the three criterion biomarkers presented in Tables 1–5. The calculated
                                   Spearman’s rho correlation coefficients of these relationships (R2 = 0.41–0.88) are considered to be moderate (Panel
                                   C) and strong (panels A and B).107 Thus, we propose the following theoretical interpretation of Figure 3 that arises from
                                   widely recognized physiological responses. Specifically, both urine concentration within the kidneys (ie, represented here
                                   by increased specific gravity) and the sensation of thirst are strongly influenced by a body water deficit (ie, elevated
                                   extracellular fluid concentration). These effects are regulated by the release of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) from
                                   the brain into the circulation,108–111 in response to increased plasma concentration, decreased plasma volume, and/or
                                   reduced arterial blood pressure.101,112 Additionally, thirst, urine concentration, and vasopressin release are influenced by
                                   oropharyngeal (ie, rear of the tongue, soft palate, and throat) nerve signals to the brain which rapidly reduce total fluid
                                   intake and modulate satiety,113,114 often before blood volume–concentration–pressure changes occur. We believe that
                                   these interrelated responses account for the strong correlation shown in Figure 3.
                                       Although an acute body mass change is recognized as the simplest and most accurate index of hydration status when
                                   serial measurements are collected in close proximity (as noted above), multiple factors influence the extent of this

                                                                                                                                                              Armstrong et al


                                   change.115,116 To explore the possibility that body mass change may not be significantly correlated with urine specific
                                   gravity or thirst, we analyzed the data in Tables 1 and 2. Both the relationship between body mass change and urine
                                   specific gravity (r = 0.50, p = 0.013), as well as the relationship between body mass change and rating of thirst (r = 0.68,
                                   p = 0.001), were significantly correlated. The strength of these two relationships are interpreted as fair and moderately
                                   strong, respectively.107,117
                                       The findings described in the three previous paragraphs demonstrate that our three criterion hydration biomarkers
                                   responded consistently when a body water deficit occurred; this suggests satisfactory internal validity. Two individual
                                   exceptions to this observation appear in Table 3, in the form of cyclists who experienced exertional hyponatremia during
                                   a 164-km summer ultraendurance event. Row 1 of Table 3 shows that the comparison group with normal serum sodium
                                   levels (column 4) consumed an average of 5.9 L of fluid during 9.0 h of cycling. In contrast, the hyponatremic cyclists
                                   A and B consumed 13.7 L/8.9 h and 14.7 L/10.6 h, respectively, which resulted in serum sodium concentrations of
                                   130 mmol/L for both27 – well below the range observed among healthy adults (136–145 mmol/L).67 In terms of body
                                   mass, the comparison group lost 1.3%, cyclist A gained 4.3%, and cyclist B experienced virtually no change of body
                                   mass (+0.1%). This obvious difference among the two hyponatremic cyclists (ie, who had identical pre- and post-ride
                                   serum sodium values) likely resulted from a large difference in their sweat rates and the fact that cyclist B rode
                                   1.7 h longer than cyclist A. It is noteworthy that both cyclists A and B exhibited post-ride urine specific gravities and
                                   thirst ratings that were well below the mean values of the comparison group (column 4). This illustrates an important
                                   concept. Due to the complex interactions of many factors, some cases of exertional hyponatremia involve body mass gain
                                   (ie, overhydration and water retention that exceeds sweat, urine, and respiratory water losses),118,119 whereas other cases
                                   are associated with a large unreplaced sweat sodium loss and partially-replaced water loss.120–122 Thus, the development
                                   of exertional hyponatremia in cyclists A and B (Table 3) and the responses of hydration biomarkers were idiosyncratic.27

                                   Considerations for Developing an IHP
                                   Previous publications describe (a) the negative effects which fluid–electrolyte imbalances can have on athletic perfor­
                                   mance, physiological functions, and health;3,4,46,51 and (b) the importance of developing an IHP for each athlete,123 as
                                   opposed to utilizing a single hydration biomarker value or a narrow range of values to indicate the threshold of
                                   detrimental effects for all athletes.84,98 In its simplest form, an IHP involves measuring an athlete’s sweat rate (described
                                   in the section titled “Body mass”) and planning the appropriate volume and timing of fluid intake in view of the
                                   anticipated rehydration opportunities of the sport. More sophisticated IHP models take into account an athlete’s tolerance
                                   to consuming a relatively large fluid volume,41 the concentration of electrolytes in sweat (ie, sodium, chloride,
                                   potassium),124,125 or the events that require sodium and carbohydrate in rehydration fluids.51,122,126 An IHP that
                                   incorporates most or all of these factors increases the likelihood that an athlete will attain the desirable middle ground
                                   between underhydration and overhydration, thereby optimizing performance.

                                   Interpreting Biomarker Data
                                   The hydration biomarker data in Tables 1–5 are intended to be used concurrently with other information to interpret changes
                                   of hydration status. Because no single biomarker accurately indicates hydration status for all athletes, activities, and
                                   environments, and because different biomarkers sometimes provide conflicting information (ie, due to the dynamic
                                   complexity of human fluid–electrolyte regulation29–33), it is best to employ information from multiple sources to determine
                                   hydration status.31–55 One common technique involves comparing an athlete’s biomarker information to a single static
                                   value that represents the threshold of detrimental effects attributed to dehydration; in fact, most sport nutrition and human
                                   hydration publications4,44–50 provide a single biomarker value (eg, urine specific gravity of 1.020) or a narrow range of
                                   values (eg, body mass loss of 3–4%) for all athletes, activities, and environments. As a second source of information, each
                                   athlete can maintain a personal diary of body weight, urine specific gravity, and thirst measurements, before and after
                                   exercise; with this data, he/she can monitor trends across days and weeks to develop personalized reference values
                                   representing usual body weight changes, urine specific gravities, and thirst ratings. This diary of past hydration experiences
                                   can then be compared to each new competition or daily training session. The biomarker data of the present review
                                   represents a third source of information. Tables 1–5 provide activity-specific values which can be utilized by athletes,

566	                                    Armstrong et al

568	
569	                                   coaches, clinicians, and physiologists as one source of information to interpret IHP effectiveness. Changes (pre- versus
570	                                   post-exercise) of an athlete’s body mass, urine specific gravity, and thirst can be compared to the hydration biomarker
571	                                   averages in Tables 1–5, to determine if those changes are typical of that sport or activity; if dehydration, euhydration (ie,
572	                                   optimal body water balance), or overhydration exist; and the extent of body water loss or gain experienced (ie, departure
573	                                   from average values). Further, athletes and coaches who have not collected hydration biomarker data previously can refer to
574	                                   the values in Tables 1–5 for a general idea of what to expect when they begin measurements.
575	                                       With regard to the practical application of data in Tables 2–5, we offer four additional observations. First, the various
576	                                   methods of making weight in combat sports (Table 2) all result in dehydration and loss of body mass. Thus, during the process of
577	                                   restoring body mass to the pre-exercise level, we recommend that measurements of our three criterion biomarkers be scheduled
578	                                   throughout the refeeding and rehydration process. Second, in cases of overhydration (Table 3), changes of biomarker values may
579	                                   differ from one athlete to the next, depending on the volume and rate of fluid intake, sweat rate, body size, duration of exercise,
580	                                   and other factors.27 We recommend that a sports medicine physician be consulted if body mass increases and if urine specific
581	                                   gravity is unusually low post-exercise, suggesting retention of excess water; also refer to the section titled “Avoiding over­
582	                                   hydration”. Third, body mass tends to be lower in the morning, whereas first morning urine specific gravity and rating of thirst
583	                                   tend to be greater than midday and afternoon values, as shown in Table 4. If measurements are recorded at various times of
584	                                   the day, they may be confounded by water and food intake, voiding, exercise, and internal circadian rhythms.95 Thus, we
585	                                   recommend day-to-day consistency in the time of measurements.31,76 Fourth, as illustrated in Table 5, ordinary daily activities
586	                                   with no exercise can influence an athlete’s body water balance. To ensure that she/he begins a competitive event or daily training
587	                                   session well-hydrated, morning measurements of the three criterion variables should guide pre-exercise fluid intake.
588	                                       The following points present additional insights regarding the interpretation of biomarker data.
589	
590	                                        ● To discover an athlete’s typical patterns of fluid loss and fluid intake, several observations should be made in
591	                                          conjunction with training sessions and relevant field simulations of competitive events.
592	                                        ● Because our three criterion biomarkers reflect the responses of different organ systems, it is possible that one
593	                                          hydration index indicates a water excess whereas the other two indices suggest a water deficit. In this case, the
594	                                          majority indication should be utilized until another assessment is completed a few hours later.124
595	                                        ● When extreme or chronic biomarker changes are observed, consider possible causes and repeat measurements at
596	                                          regular intervals. If values do not return to pre-exercise levels within a reasonable time frame, consult a physician.
597	
598	                                   Body Mass
599	                                        ● During exercise lasting 0.5–4.0 h, body mass change is the most commonly used representation of body water loss
600	                                          or gain36,39 because muscle mass and adipose tissue changes are negligible.
601	                                        ● We recommend using the same digital floor scale each time that body mass is measured. Many floor scales can be
602	                                          calibrated by following the manufacturer’s instructions and loading the scale with objects of known mass. Identical
603	                                          clothing and footwear should be worn during each measurement. A digital floor scale that reads to ±100 g has
604	                                          a measurement resolution of ±0.1 L (eg, 100 mL out of a 42–47 L total body water volume).
605	                                        ● An athlete’s sweat rate (ie, the volume of sweat produced per hour, expressed as L/h or qt/h) is determined by
606	                                          measuring pre-exercise nude body mass and exercising for 60 min (ie, in an environment, at an exercise intensity,
607	                                          and wearing clothing/equipment that simulates a future event). After exercise, nude post-exercise body mass, with
608	                                          sweat wiped from the skin, is subtracted from the pre-exercise body mass and corrected for fluid consumed and
609	                                          urine eliminated, if any.41,51,124 Additional details regarding the calculation of sweat rate, plus the methods for
610	                                          measuring sweat electrolyte losses (eg, sodium, potassium), appear elsewhere.41,124
611	                                        ● Sweat electrolyte losses become problematic during events lasting more than 4 h (ie, due to an increased risk of
612	                                          exertional hyponatremia) or across consecutive days of heavy sweating with inadequate dietary water and sodium
613	                                          replacement.24,41,51
614	                                        ● To assess the day-to-day change of body mass, measurements should be compared to the baseline body mass for
615	                                          that individual. To determine this baseline, measure morning body mass on 3–5 consecutive days.85 The median
616	                                          (middle) or average body mass serves as a meaningful baseline for that individual.124 If the body mass value on the
617	
618	
619	                                   40         https://doi.org/10.2147/OAJSM.S508656                                        Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine 2025:16
620	
621	
622	
623	Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org)
624	                                                                                                                                                               Armstrong et al
625	
626	
627	                                        morning after an endurance event is notably less or greater than baseline, fluid intake should be adjusted
628	                                        accordingly (ie, avoiding overconsumption and underconsumption) for 24–48 h.75,127
629	                                      ● Two other considerations are relevant. First, if dietary “carbohydrate loading” is employed during the days prior to
630	                                        competition, the baseline body mass may increase (0.5–1.5 kg) because water is stored with glycogen in skeletal
631	                                        muscles. Second, body mass measurements may not be valid after an event lasting 7–24 h because cellular water is
632	                                        generated during metabolic reactions, and skeletal muscle or adipose tissue is degraded.51,115,128,129
633	
634	                                   Urine Specific Gravity
635	                                   When a total body water deficit exists, the kidneys retain water by concentrating urine and decreasing urine volume; in
636	                                   contrast, when excess fluid has been consumed and retained, a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. These changes
637	                                   (ie, dehydration or fluid overload) can be detected by observing urine samples.
638	
639	                                      ● Urine specific gravity is recommended as a practical and valid biomarker for identifying suboptimal fluid intake or
640	                                        underhydration by professional sports medicine organizations,3,4,46 physiologists, and researchers.6,76,89,97,130–132
641	                                      ● Urine specific gravity (see Tables 1–5, Figures 2 and 3) is measured quickly and accurately with a refractometer.75,133
642	                                        This instrument is relatively inexpensive, simple to use, and is available from online retail platforms as a handheld
643	                                        device which can be calibrated before use.
644	                                      ● An euhydrated urine specific gravity baseline value (ie, usually between 1.015 and 1.02526,27) should be determined
645	                                        for each athlete, using a method similar to the one described above for body weight. Changes from this baseline
646	                                        value will assist the interpretation of hydration status.
647	                                      ● Hydration assessment via urine specific gravity has limitations when used alone,90,98,134 as do all hydration
648	                                        biomarkers.
649	                                      ● Many athletes consume nutritional supplements to gain a performance edge or health benefit.135–138 When
650	                                        consumed in the manufacturer’s recommended dosage, supplements such as vitamin C, beetroot, and riboflavin
651	                                        may or may not alter urine color.139,140 However, even if they visibly alter urine color, it is unlikely that nutritional
652	                                        supplements will measurably influence urine specific gravity because the mass and osmolar content of nutritional
653	                                        supplements is small in comparison to the total osmolar load of the food items in an athlete’s daily diet.30
654	                                      ● During normal daily activities, men may78,79,141 or may not69,70 exhibit a greater urine specific gravity than women.
655	                                      ● An analysis of data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES; n = 3,634) indicated
656	                                        that urine specific gravity is influenced by body size and body composition.142 Thus, athletes who have a large lean
657	                                        body mass or body mass index can be expected to have greater urine specific gravity values than their smaller
658	                                        counterparts.
659	                                      ● If an athlete consumes a large volume of pure water or dilute beverage rapidly (eg, 1.4 L in 30 minutes), urine
660	                                        specific gravity decreases (eg, < 1.010) in both well-hydrated and dehydrated athletes as a defense against fluid
661	                                        overload.97 In contrast, if the same volume of water or dilute fluid is consumed gradually and in small aliquots, the
662	                                        change of urine specific gravity will be minor.30,115,119 The sensation of thirst exhibits a parallel phenomenon.
663	
664	                                   Rating of Thirst
665	                                   As noted above, thirst is a sensation that regulates total body water and the concentration of body fluids. Coordinated by
666	                                   the brain, thirst responds in concert with renal responses to correct fluid and electrolyte perturbations. Figure 3 illustrates
667	                                   the relationships between thirst, urine specific gravity, and body mass loss. In particular, panel A supports our
668	                                   recommendation to assess subjective ratings of thirst.
669	
670	                                      ● In research studies involving a variety of activities, thirst ratings have consistently identified an existing body water
671	                                         deficit. See Figure 2.
672	                                      ● Thirst is initially sensed when a body mass loss of 1–2% occurs during exercise-heat stress,11,32 or when a 0.5%
673	                                         body mass loss occurs during routine daily activities involving no exercise,23 and intensifies as the body water
674	                                         deficit increases.
675	
676	
677	                                   Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine 2025:16                                                https://doi.org/10.2147/OAJSM.S508656
678	                                                                                                                                                                         41
679	
680	
681	Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org)
682	                                    Armstrong et al
683	
684	
685	                                        ● Research has shown that the morning sensation of thirst upon waking is a reliable indicator of hydration status.76,143
686	                                          However, an intense morning sensation of thirst may not affect body mass, total water intake, or hydration status
687	                                          later in the day.69
688	                                        ● We recommend measuring thirst with a 9-point intensity rating scale63 because of its simplicity. This scale offers the
689	                                          following options: 1, not thirsty at all; 3, a little thirsty; 5, moderately thirsty; 7, very thirsty; and 9, very very
690	                                          thirsty. See Tables 1–4 and Figure 3.
691	                                        ● An euhydrated baseline thirst rating should be determined for each athlete, using a method similar to the one
692	                                          described above for body weight. Changes from this baseline value will assist the interpretation of hydration status.
693	                                        ● Field studies have reported that thirst was not correlated with the hydration status of youth campers144 and high
694	                                          school football players.145 This may be due to an age-related difference of thirst (ie, influenced by puberty and
695	                                          maturation). Alternatively, these observations may be due to the difficulty of controlling pre-exercise hydration state
696	                                          or fluid intake throughout the day, in a field setting. This matter requires further investigation to determine its
697	                                          relevance to the thirst responses of young athletes.
698	
699	                                   Strategies for Drinking During Exercise
700	                                        ● An important component of each IHP is the amount of fluid which an athlete can gain access to during training or
701	                                          competition.41 If an athlete has unrestricted access, consuming the appropriate amount of fluid is relatively easy.
702	                                          However, the rules of many sporting events (eg, tennis) do not allow continuous access to fluids; this challenges the

802	                                        ● During ordinary daily activities, the average body mass may be lower in the morning (whereas urine specific gravity
803	                                          and thirst values tend to be greater) than during afternoon hours (Table 4). However, because exceptions have been

808	                                          average body mass loss of 1.1% was observed in healthy young men after only 8.5 h of water restriction (Table 5).

822	                                   Summary
823	                                   The hydration biomarker changes in Tables 1–5 provide reference values that can be compared to an athlete’s body
824	                                   weight, urine specific gravity, and thirst sensation. These reference values are intended to be used as one component of
825	                                   a comprehensive IHP. Such comparisons enhance the interpretation of both pre- and post-exercise measurements
826	                                   uniquely, by providing a window into the past experiences of athletes during outdoor events, weight category sports,
827	                                   training sessions, and routine daily activities. This repository of sport-relevant hydration biomarker data is unique in the
828	                                   extant literature because it does not rely on single threshold values (ie, one value fits all). We propose that consistent use
829	                                   of these reference values, as part of a multi-faceted IHP, will clarify the extent of dehydration or overhydration, guide
830	                                   rehydration efforts, and optimize subsequent exercise performance, recovery, and health.

                                   methods of making weight in combat sports (Table 2) all result in dehydration and loss of body mass. Thus, during the process of
                                   restoring body mass to the pre-exercise level, we recommend that measurements of our three criterion biomarkers be scheduled
                                   throughout the refeeding and rehydration process. Second, in cases of overhydration (Table 3), changes of biomarker values may
                                   differ from one athlete to the next, depending on the volume and rate of fluid intake, sweat rate, body size, duration of exercise,
                                   and other factors.27 We recommend that a sports medicine physician be consulted if body mass increases and if urine specific
                                   gravity is unusually low post-exercise, suggesting retention of excess water; also refer to the section titled “Avoiding over­
                                   hydration”. Third, body mass tends to be lower in the morning, whereas first morning urine specific gravity and rating of thirst
                                   tend to be greater than midday and afternoon values, as shown in Table 4. If measurements are recorded at various times of
                                   the day, they may be confounded by water and food intake, voiding, exercise, and internal circadian rhythms.95 Thus, we
                                   recommend day-to-day consistency in the time of measurements.31,76 Fourth, as illustrated in Table 5, ordinary daily activities
                                   with no exercise can influence an athlete’s body water balance. To ensure that she/he begins a competitive event or daily training

                                          regular intervals. If values do not return to pre-exercise levels within a reasonable time frame, consult a physician.

                                          calibrated by following the manufacturer’s instructions and loading the scale with objects of known mass. Identical
                                          clothing and footwear should be worn during each measurement. A digital floor scale that reads to ±100 g has
                                          a measurement resolution of ±0.1 L (eg, 100 mL out of a 42–47 L total body water volume).

                                   Urine Specific Gravity
                                   When a total body water deficit exists, the kidneys retain water by concentrating urine and decreasing urine volume; in
                                   contrast, when excess fluid has been consumed and retained, a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. These changes
                                   (ie, dehydration or fluid overload) can be detected by observing urine samples.

                                        underhydration by professional sports medicine organizations,3,4,46 physiologists, and researchers.6,76,89,97,130–132
                                      ● Urine specific gravity (see Tables 1–5, Figures 2 and 3) is measured quickly and accurately with a refractometer.75,133
                                        This instrument is relatively inexpensive, simple to use, and is available from online retail platforms as a handheld
                                        device which can be calibrated before use.
                                      ● An euhydrated urine specific gravity baseline value (ie, usually between 1.015 and 1.02526,27) should be determined
                                        for each athlete, using a method similar to the one described above for body weight. Changes from this baseline
                                        value will assist the interpretation of hydration status.
                                      ● Hydration assessment via urine specific gravity has limitations when used alone,90,98,134 as do all hydration
                                        biomarkers.
                                      ● Many athletes consume nutritional supplements to gain a performance edge or health benefit.135–138 When
                                        consumed in the manufacturer’s recommended dosage, supplements such as vitamin C, beetroot, and riboflavin
                                        may or may not alter urine color.139,140 However, even if they visibly alter urine color, it is unlikely that nutritional
                                        supplements will measurably influence urine specific gravity because the mass and osmolar content of nutritional
                                        supplements is small in comparison to the total osmolar load of the food items in an athlete’s daily diet.30

                                        specific gravity decreases (eg, < 1.010) in both well-hydrated and dehydrated athletes as a defense against fluid
                                        overload.97 In contrast, if the same volume of water or dilute fluid is consumed gradually and in small aliquots, the
                                        change of urine specific gravity will be minor.30,115,119 The sensation of thirst exhibits a parallel phenomenon.

                                         body mass loss occurs during routine daily activities involving no exercise,23 and intensifies as the body water
                                         deficit increases.

                                      ● During the week following competition, an investigation of Australian Olympic combat sports161 revealed that
                                        athletes regained considerable body weight (eg, boxing, 4.1%; judo, 3.6%; taekwondo, 4.6%; and wrestling, 4.8%
                                        of their baseline body mass).
                                      ● We recommend downloading a copy of the 2021 American College of Sports Medicine consensus statement which
                                        focuses on weight-category sports.159 This document contains a wealth of information regarding the benefits and
                                        disadvantages of weight-making practices, pre-event weigh-in procedures, opportunities for recovery after weigh-in,
                                        sport rule changes to minimize potential harmful effects of making weight, and recommendations for safer weight-
                                        making practices in various sports.

                                   Routine Daily Activities
                                        ● During ordinary daily activities, the average body mass may be lower in the morning (whereas urine specific gravity
                                          and thirst values tend to be greater) than during afternoon hours (Table 4). However, because exceptions have been
                                          reported,69 the morning body mass of each athlete should be recorded in a personal diary each day, to determine his/
                                          her unique responses.
                                        ● Most humans do not experience severe dehydration (> 5% body mass loss) during routine daily activities but may
                                          reach a state of mild dehydration (1–2% of body mass lost as water) multiple times each week.30 For example, an
                                          average body mass loss of 1.1% was observed in healthy young men after only 8.5 h of water restriction (Table 5).
                                        ● For reasons that have not been clarified, some individuals habitually consume little water each day.30 These low
                                          volume drinkers (plain water + beverages + food moisture < 1.5 L/24 h) represent 25–33% of all adults in the
                                          United States and Europe.162–164 This 1.5 L volume is considerably less than the Adequate Intakes for water
                                          recommended by the European Food Safety Authority165 and the US National Academy of Medicine166 for men
                                          (2.5, 3.7 L/d) and for women (2.0, 2.7 L/d).
                                        ● A 2024 review paper167 reported that chronic low volume drinking behavior, and/or urine biomarkers that signal
                                          chronic dehydration, are strongly associated with two disease states: type 2 diabetes and kidney stones.
                                        ● The four preceding observations emphasize that hydration practices during routine daily activities are an important
                                          aspect of an athlete’s hydration state. To ensure that she/he begins a competitive event or training session well-
                                          hydrated, the pre-exercise biomarker values in Tables 1–4 can be utilized to interpret an athlete’s hydration status
                                          prior to exercise.


                                   Summary
                                   The hydration biomarker changes in Tables 1–5 provide reference values that can be compared to an athlete’s body
                                   weight, urine specific gravity, and thirst sensation. These reference values are intended to be used as one component of
                                   a comprehensive IHP. Such comparisons enhance the interpretation of both pre- and post-exercise measurements
                                   uniquely, by providing a window into the past experiences of athletes during outdoor events, weight category sports,
                                   training sessions, and routine daily activities. This repository of sport-relevant hydration biomarker data is unique in the
                                   extant literature because it does not rely on single threshold values (ie, one value fits all). We propose that consistent use
                                   of these reference values, as part of a multi-faceted IHP, will clarify the extent of dehydration or overhydration, guide
                                   rehydration efforts, and optimize subsequent exercise performance, recovery, and health.

{
 "id":"Q26", "sourceFile":"Recurrent and subsequent injuries in professional and elite sport - A systematic review.pdf", "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Recurrent and Subsequent Injuries in Professional and Elite Sport: a Systematic Review' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury", "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury"], "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"], "sports":["Soccer","Rugby","Track & Field","Other Sport"], "populations":["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42019119264) of prospective injury surveillance studies in professional or elite football, rugby, athletics, cricket and multi-sport events, searched to July 2020. Of 81 eligible studies, 30 did not report recurrent injuries, leaving 51 for data extraction. Where recurrent injuries were reported, their proportion of all injuries ranged from 5.5% to 48%, and in the few studies using subsequent injury models most subsequent injuries (51 to 80%) were different and unrelated to the index injury.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review is limited to English-language studies of professional and elite sport with a published consensus definition, so amateur and collegiate data are excluded. Many included studies pooled data across seasons and scored low on the Downs and Black quality checklist, which limits how precisely their injury rates can be compared.",
 "synthesisCaution":"The recurrent-injury proportions describe how injuries were recorded in pooled surveillance data, not how often an individual athlete re-injures the same tissue, so they should not be read as a measured re-injury risk.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Bitchell CL, Varley-Campbell J, Robinson G, Stiles V, Mathema P, Moore IS. Recurrent and Subsequent Injuries in Professional and Elite Sport: a Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2020;6:58.",
   "doi":"10.1186/s40798-020-00286-3",
   "abstract":"Reporting of recurrent and subsequent injuries in professional and elite sport was inconsistent across 51 extracted surveillance studies, and few used subsequent injury categorisation models. In studies using those models, most subsequent injuries were to a different body part and unrelated to the index injury.",
   "tldr":"More than a third of eligible professional-sport injury surveillance studies did not report recurrent injuries at all, and few used a subsequent injury model. Staff should not assume published injury rates separate new injuries from re-injuries of the same tissue.",
   "methods":"PRISMA systematic review of prospective injury surveillance studies in professional or elite sport that followed a published consensus statement. Searches of SCOPUS, Embase and Medline covered articles published after 2005, up to 23 July 2020. Eighty-one studies met criteria, and 51 (one article containing two studies) were eligible for data extraction after excluding 30 that did not report recurrent injuries. Quality was rated with an amended Downs and Black checklist, and results were summarised narratively.",
   "findings":"Of the 51 studies, 44 reported recurrent injuries as a number, percentage, incidence or a combination, with proportions ranging from 5.5% to 48% and incidence from 0.5 to 2.55 per 1000 h. Seven studies used subsequent injury terminology, and 51 to 80% of subsequent injuries were classed as different and unrelated to the index injury. Specific subsequent injury categorisation models were used in only three studies.",
   "limitations":"Only one level of sport (professional or elite) and English-language studies were included, so amateur, collegiate and non-English data were excluded. Many studies pooled injuries across several seasons without reporting the number of new participants each season, and quality scores were often low. The review did not pool effect sizes.",
   "practicalImplications":"Injury reports from professional sport should be checked for whether they separate recurrent from new injuries, and for how many players and seasons they cover. Where a subsequent injury model is available, it gives more specific information on which injuries follow an earlier one.",
   "athleteDev":"The review does not evaluate any training intervention. Its relevance for athlete development is limited to how injury data are recorded and interpreted when comparing squads or seasons.",
   "rtp":"The review reports how recurrent and subsequent injuries are recorded in professional sport, but it does not give return-to-play timelines, criteria or outcomes. It cannot be used to decide whether an athlete is ready to return or how long recovery should take."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "evidenceSummary/findings: 'recurrent injuries made up 5 to 21% of injuries' conflated with the across-study range -> recurrent proportion across the 44 reporting studies is 5.5% to 48% ('the proportion ranged from 5.5 [81] to 48% [59]'); the abstract's 5 to 21% figure comes from subsequent-injury-model categories and is no longer stated as a share of all injuries",
     "tldr: 'Most ... studies do not report whether injuries are recurrent' -> more than a third did not (30 of 81, '30 (37%) of these articles did not report the recurrence of injuries')",
     "abstract: removed the 5 to 21% statement for the same reason",
     "synthesisCaution: reworded to refer to recurrent-injury proportions generally rather than the 5 to 21% range"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"The abstract's 'proportion of recurrent injuries ... ranged from 5 to 21%' is not clearly reconciled with the results section (5.5% to 48%); the record now reports the results-section range.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q28", "sourceFile":"Redefining the draft pick valuation in the National Football League.pdf", "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Redefining the draft pick valuation in the National Football League' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Other",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance", "domains":["Training & Performance"], "audiences":["Research & Analytics","Coaching"], "sports":["American Football"], "populations":["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A retrospective brief research report of 4,996 NFL draft picks from 1993 to 2012 (pro-football-reference.com data), using fifth-order polynomial regressions of each pick's career weighted approximate value (wAV), games played (GP) and seasons started (ST), with round-specific trade-up dummies. The authors report that Rounds 4 to 7 outperform the Jimmy Johnson pick value chart, that the last first-round pick is worth about 56% of the first pick on GP (versus 20% on the chart), and that first-round trade-ups are associated with lower wAV, GP and ST. Model 2 explains only 22 to 31% of the variance (R2).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The study measures draft value through career output of players in a single league, so it says little about training, health or injury, and it does not adjust for position, team, or the player's injury history. The trade-up models explain 22 to 31% of the variance, and trade-up effects were significant only in Round 1 (all three outcomes) and Round 4 (seasons started only).",
 "synthesisCaution":"The paper's advice to accumulate Day 3 picks rests on average career outcomes across all positions and teams, so it should not be read as a guarantee that any particular late-round pick will be a productive starter.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Hadley B, Kim JW, Magnusen M, Kim KT. Redefining the draft pick valuation in the National Football League. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2025;7:1628223.",
   "doi":"10.3389/fspor.2025.1628223",
   "abstract":"Regression models of 1993 to 2012 draft picks suggest late-round picks are undervalued by Jimmy Johnson's Pick Value Chart, and first-round trade-ups are associated with lower career wAV, games played and seasons started. The authors report a recalibrated pick value chart and a Day 3 emphasis.",
   "tldr":"Late-round NFL picks produced more career value than the classic pick value chart predicts, and first-round trade-ups were linked to weaker player outcomes. Front offices may want to test these findings against their own draft records before changing how they trade picks.",
   "methods":"Archival data from pro-football-reference.com for 4,996 draft picks from 1993 to 2012. Model 1 averaged each of 262 pick slots and fitted fifth-order polynomial regressions to wAV, GP and ST. Model 2 used player-level data with seven round-specific trade-up dummies. The results are from ordinary regression with the outcome measures as reported on the source site.",
   "findings":"Model 1 R2 was 0.90 for wAV, 0.82 for GP and 0.90 for ST. The last first-round pick was valued at about 56% of the first pick on GP, versus 20% on the chart. In Model 2, first-round trade-ups had significantly lower wAV (coefficient -5.44, P = .013), GP (-13.33, P = .018) and ST (-0.82, P = .008). Round 4 trade-ups had a significant positive effect on ST (0.92, P = .011), and other rounds were not significant. Model 2 R2 was 0.31 for wAV, 0.22 for GP and 0.31 for ST.",
   "limitations":"Outcomes are career totals from a single league, and the models do not adjust for position, team, injuries, or contract status. Model 2 explains little variance, and the round-specific effects are inconsistent (only Round 1 and Round 4 reach significance, with Round 4 effects visible only on ST). The paper does not test whether a recalibrated chart improves real draft results. The authors note that financial constraints can also shape draft behaviour.",
   "practicalImplications":"Draft boards may want to give more weight to later-round picks than the classic chart does, and first-round trade-ups should be checked against the lower average outcomes reported here. These are average patterns across the league, so each draft decision still needs player-level evaluation.",
   "athleteDev":"The paper gives no development or training data. Its relevance is to how teams value young players drafted from college and how they assess career output across positions.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable. The study does not examine injury, rehabilitation or return to play."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "screeningLimitations: 'trade-up effects are small' -> effects were not small in Round 1 (GP coefficient -13.33); now states they were significant only in Round 1 (all outcomes) and Round 4 (ST only, P = .011)",
     "evidenceSummary: noted article type ('TYPE Brief Research Report')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Eligibility is borderline: this is front-office draft valuation analytics, not athlete health or performance evidence in the usual sense. Kept INCLUDE because it is original research on sport, but a reviewer may prefer EXCLUDE (c). The text also gives both 1993 to 2012 and 1994 to 2012 for the averaged dataset.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q30", "sourceFile":"Reduced match exposure in the previous 2 matches accounts for hamstring muscle injury incidence in professional football players.pdf", "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Reduced Match Exposure in the Previous 2 Matches Accounts for Hamstring Muscle Injury Incidence in Professional Football Players' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Case-control Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury", "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"], "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance"], "sports":["Soccer"], "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A prospective controlled observational study over three LaLiga seasons in two professional teams. Thirty-seven hamstring strain injuries in 23 outfield players were each paired 1:1 with an uninjured starter in the same position and team. Lower cumulative playing time, distance and high-speed running in the one and two matches before injury were associated with higher injury risk (for example, playing time relative risk 1.41 per 10 min in the match before injury), while the three- and four-match windows were not significant for playing time.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Training load was not recorded, and injuries occurred in both matches (86.4%) and training (13.6%). Data came from two teams over three seasons, and the cut-off points have low sensitivity (36% to 64%), so many injured players would not have been flagged.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Low match minutes in the previous two games were linked with hamstring injury, but this is an association in matched pairs from two teams, and the cut-offs should not be used as a screening threshold that predicts which individual player will be injured.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Moreno-Pérez V, Del Coso J, López-Del Campo R, Resta R, Romero-Sangüesa J, Courel-Ibáñez J, et al. Reduced Match Exposure in the Previous 2 Matches Accounts for Hamstring Muscle Injury Incidence in Professional Football Players. Sports Health. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1177/19417381231158117",
   "abstract":"Hamstring strain injuries in 37 professional players were associated with lower playing time, total running and high-speed running in the one and two matches before injury, compared with paired uninjured controls. Playing time of 64 minutes or less in the match before injury was one practical cut-off.",
   "tldr":"In professional football, a hamstring strain was more likely after a player had very little match exposure in the two games before it. Playing minutes are a simple metric that staff can track to flag players with recent low match load.",
   "methods":"Prospective controlled observational study of 144 outfield players from two LaLiga teams over three seasons. Thirty-seven noncontact hamstring strains were each matched 1:1 to an uninjured starter in the same team and position. Playing time, total distance and high-speed running (above 24 km/h) were taken from a video tracking system for the four matches before injury. Generalized estimating equations gave relative risks, and ROC analysis gave diagnostic accuracy.",
   "findings":"Injured players had lower playing time, distance and high-speed running in the match before injury (for example, 65.4 vs 88.5 min playing time) and in the two matches before injury. Playing time relative risk was 1.41 per 10 min in one match and 1.14 per 10 min across two matches. Cut-offs in the match before injury were high-speed running of 328 m or less (sensitivity 64%, specificity 84%) and playing time of 64 min or less (sensitivity 36%, specificity 97%). Windows of three and four matches showed no significant differences in playing time.",
   "limitations":"Training exposure and internal load were not recorded, and injuries from training were included. Only two teams were studied, and the match-based cut-offs have high specificity but low sensitivity, so they miss many players who go on to be injured. The 3- and 4-match windows were not significant for playing time, and the authors suggest underexposure need not be sustained over longer periods to matter, but the study does not test a mechanism. The time taken to complete the four matches before injury differed between players, although the match before injury was 3 to 7 days before it for all players.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff could record playing minutes for each player's last two matches and flag players with very low recent minutes for closer monitoring and individual load planning. The cut-off of about 64 minutes in the previous match was the most specific measure in this sample, but it misses many injuries and should be tested in other squads before being used as a rule.",
   "athleteDev":"The study supports tracking match minutes and high-speed running in the previous two matches as part of individual load management for players with reduced match involvement. It does not test training programmes that prevent hamstring injury.",
   "rtp":"The study does not assess return-to-play criteria and did not study players returning from injury. It cannot be used to set how quickly match minutes are reintroduced after an injury."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "screeningLimitations: 'cut-off points have low specificity, so many players with low exposure are not injured' -> low sensitivity (Table/abstract: 'sensitivity, 64%; specificity, 84%', 'sensitivity, 36%; specificity, 97%')",
     "limitations: 'low specificity, so they produce many false positives' -> high specificity, low sensitivity, so many injured players are missed; clarified the 3- to 7-day note as the authors' timing limitation",
     "athleteDev: 'players returning to or returning from reduced match involvement' -> 'players with reduced match involvement'",
     "rtp: removed speculative advice on reintroducing match minutes after injury (study did not examine returning players)"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"The Table 1 footnote says RR is per unit increase in exposure ('for a given increase in the exposure, the chances of injury increased'), which contradicts the reported direction (lower exposure, higher risk). The record keeps the RR values as printed; a reviewer may check the direction wording.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}
